Math.title: Use equivalent ratios
Math.subject: Math
Math.instructions: Study the ratio table and worked examples before solving. Keep the order of the two quantities the same.
Math.explanation: A ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. Equivalent ratios describe the same relationship. To make an equivalent ratio, multiply or divide both quantities by the same nonzero number. If blue beads to yellow beads is 2 to 5, multiplying both parts by 1.5 gives 3 to 7.5. Multiplying both by 2 gives 4 to 10. The relationship stays the same because both parts change by the same factor.

workedExamples.title: Find a value equivalent to 2:5 when the first amount is 3
steps: The first amount changes from 2 to 3, so multiply by 1.5.
Multiply the second amount by the same factor: 5 × 1.5 = 7.5.

workedExamples.title: Scale 4:7 by a factor of 3
steps: Multiply the second part by the same factor: 7 × 3 = 21.

visuals.alt: A ratio table shows 2 blue beads to 5 yellow beads and an equivalent 3 to 7.5 ratio.
visuals.caption: Both parts scale by the same factor.

English.title: A myth: Theseus and the labyrinth
English.subject: English
English.instructions: Read this original summary of one ancient Greek myth. Myths have different versions; answer from this version and inspect the historical vase image as a separate source.
English.passage: In one ancient Greek story, Theseus enters a winding labyrinth where the Minotaur lives. He carries a thread given to him so he can trace a path back through the confusing passages. The story focuses on a difficult task, a risk, and a plan to return safely. A plan does not remove every danger, but it can help a character respond to a problem. Ancient artists also showed scenes from myths on pottery. A painted vase is a historical object: it can provide clues about how an artist represented a story, but one picture does not tell every part of the tale.

visuals.alt: Ancient Greek vase painting showing the mythic figures Theseus and the Minotaur.
visuals.caption: A historical image related to the myth; compare what the scene shows with what the passage explains.

Science.title: Model the parts of an animal cell
Science.subject: Science
Science.instructions: Read the explanation and use the labeled model. The model is simplified and not drawn to scale.
Science.passage: A cell is the basic unit of living things. In an animal cell, the cell membrane forms a boundary and helps control what enters and leaves. Cytoplasm fills much of the cell, and many cell processes happen there. The nucleus contains genetic material and helps direct cell activities. Cells contain other structures too; this simple model shows only three parts. Plant cells share some of these parts and also have structures such as a cell wall and chloroplasts.

visuals.alt: A simplified animal cell model labels the cell membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus.
visuals.caption: The diagram is a model; real cells are far more detailed and are not this shape or scale.

Science.modelTask: Draw an animal cell and label its membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus. Then add a short note describing one job of each labeled part.

Social Studies.title: How river valleys supported early communities
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.instructions: Read the passage and study the 1890 map. Separate what the map shows from what the passage explains.
Social Studies.passage: The Nile River runs through northeastern Africa and flows north toward the Mediterranean Sea. Water, fertile soils in some areas, and routes for travel helped people build communities along the river. People also had to respond to floods, dry regions, and changing conditions. A river valley can offer resources, but people still make choices about farming, building, trade, and leadership. This historic 1890 map represents ancient Egypt; it can help you locate the Nile, but it is not a modern map and should be treated as a source with a date and creator.

visuals.caption: Trace the Nile and its delta. The map is a historical representation, not a current political map.
